questionText: The set of all recursively enumerable languages is
options: a subset of the set of all recursive languages.
explanation:
Analysis of Options:

Option (A): Incorrect. Recursively Enumerable (RE) languages are not closed under complementation. If a language $L$ and its complement $\bar{L}$ are both RE, then $L$ is recursive.

Option (B): Correct. RE languages are closed under intersection. If $L_1$ and $L_2$ are recognized by Turing machines $M_1$ and $M_2$, we can construct a Turing machine $M$ that simulates both $M_1$ and $M_2$. $M$ accepts if and only if both $M_1$ and $M_2$ accept. Thus, $L_1 \cap L_2$ is also RE.

Option (C): Incorrect. Every recursive language is recursively enumerable, which means recursive languages are a proper subset of RE languages ($\text{Recursive} \subset \text{RE}$), not the other way around.

Option (D): Incorrect. Every RE language is accepted by a Turing machine. Since every Turing machine can be uniquely encoded as a finite binary string, the set of all Turing machines—and consequently the set of all RE languages—is countably infinite, not uncountable.
